claims.source: Inference from the January 1953 panel recommendations against the August 1953 and August 1954 regulation editions
claims.text: AFR 200-2 is the Robertson Panel's debunking recommendation converted into binding internal law seven months after the panel reported.

The 1953 edition exists in a readable four-page scan whose face reads 'AIR FORCE REGULATION NO. 200-2 / DEPARTMENT OF THE AIR FORCE / WASHINGTON, 26 AUGUST 1953 / INTELLIGENCE / (Unclassified) Unidentified Flying Objects Reporting (Short Title: UFOB)', marked RESTRICTED / SECURITY INFORMATION and signed 'By Order of the Secretary of the Air Force: N. F. TWINING, Chief of Staff'.

claims.source: AFR 200-2, 26 August 1953, footnote to the title and marginal annotations
claims.text: Its own footnote establishes the predecessor: 'This Regulation supersedes AFL 200-5, 29 April 1952.' The release copy also carries handwritten annotations 'Sup by AFR 200-2, 12 Aug 54' and 'amended by 200-2A' against paragraph 6.

claims.source: AFR 200-2, 26 August 1953, paragraph 8, Release of Information
claims.text: The release restriction is on the face of the 1953 edition, not only the 1954 one. Paragraph 8 provides that raw information may be furnished to a public information officer 'except names of principals, Air Force comments, details of intercept procedures involved, and classified radar data', and that what is releasable ends at 'The fact that the object has been conclusively identified by ATIC as a conventional aerial device or other familiar object and no further evaluation is contemplated.' Identified cases could be discussed publicly; unidentified ones could not.

Paragraph 7 provides that 'All evidence will be forwarded to ATIC', and on materiel directs units to 'Safeguard the materiel carefully to prevent any defacing or alteration which would reduce its value for technical analysis' and to 'Notify ATIC immediately and request shipping instructions'.

claims.source: AFR 200-2, 12 August 1954, footnote and paragraph text
claims.text: The 1954 edition's own footnote closes the chain: 'This Regulation supersedes AFR 200-2, 26 August 1953, Including Change 200-2A, 2 November 1953.' Its short title changed from UFOB to FLYOBRPT and it added the 4602d AISS to the investigation chain, which the 1953 edition does not name.

desc: AFR 200-2, 'Unidentified Flying Objects Reporting', is the internal Air Force regulation that operationalised the Robertson Panel's recommendations seven months after the panel reported. The 12 August 1954 edition, superseding the 26 August 1953 edition, sets out the reporting chain — base level to Air Defense Command, field investigation by the 4602d Air Intelligence Service Squadron, terminal analysis at ATIC, Wright-Patterson — and, critically, governs what may be said publicly. Its release policy states that for objects which are not explainable, 'only the fact that ATIC will analyze the data is worthy of release, due to many unknowns involved', and protects names of principals, intercept and investigation procedures, and classified radar data. In plain terms: solved cases could be discussed, unsolved cases could not. Every public Air Force statement of the period that unexplained cases were unimportant was made under a regulation forbidding officers from discussing them. The regulation was issued under the tenure of Gen. Nathan Twining as Chief of Staff — the same officer who had written in 1947 that the phenomenon was real.

timeline.label: AFR 200-2 puts the release restriction in writing
timeline.text: Air Force Regulation 200-2, short title UFOB, signed by order of the Secretary of the Air Force by N. F. Twining, supersedes AFL 200-5 of 29 April 1952. It designates ATIC as the analysis authority, directs that all evidence be forwarded there, and restricts public discussion to cases conclusively identified as conventional. Identified cases could be discussed; unidentified ones could not.
